notes.meaning: The tribe of Dan gave four towns to the Kohathite Levites who were not priests. These towns included open fields around them where the Levites could graze their cattle and keep livestock. Even though Dan faced strong resistance from local enemies in this coastal area, they still shared their allotted land with the Lord's servants.

The western half-tribe of Manasseh gave two towns, Taanach and Gath-rimmon, along with their surrounding fields. This completed the share given to this branch of the Kohathites from the central region of the country. God made sure that every part of the land helped support the people who cared for His worship.

In all, the non-priestly Kohathite families received ten towns from Ephraim, Dan, and western Manasseh. These Levites had the sacred duty of taking care of the holy furnishings used in God's tabernacle, His tent of worship. Having homes in these central tribes kept them close to where the tabernacle was set up.

The Gershonite clans received two towns from the eastern half-tribe of Manasseh, across the Jordan River. One of these was Golan, which served as a city of refuge where someone who killed a person by accident could flee for safety. The other was Beeshterah, a former pagan royal city that was now set apart for the Lord's ministers.

The tribe of Issachar gave four towns to the Gershonite families from the fertile Jezreel Valley. These towns provided quiet homes and fertile ground for the Levites to live among the people. God placed His ministers across regular farming communities so the people could always seek spiritual guidance.

Along with Kishion and Daberath, Issachar gave Jarmuth and En-gannim to complete their share. Each town came with open grazing land for flocks and herds. The tribe willingly gave up valuable settled places to honor God's plan for the Levites.

The northern tribe of Asher set aside four towns with their pasturelands for the Gershonites. These northern coastal towns brought God's ministers all the way to the far borders of the nation. No tribe was left out of the duty or the blessing of supporting God's work.

The tribe of Naphtali provided three towns in the northern hills for the Gershonites. One of them was Kedesh in Galilee, which also served as a city of refuge for the northern region. God made sure that both spiritual teachers and places of mercy were easily reached by everyone.

The Gershonite clans received thirteen towns in total, spread across northern and eastern Israel. In earlier days their main job was carrying the curtains and ropes of the sacred tent. Now they were settled throughout these northern districts to teach the people God's word.

The Merarites, the last group of Levite clans, received four towns from the tribe of Zebulun. These included Jokneam, Kartah, Dimnah, and Nahalal, together with pasturelands. In the wilderness they had carried the heavy wooden frames of the tabernacle, and now they received a peaceful home.

The tribe of Reuben, living east of the Jordan River, gave four towns to the Merarites. One of these was Bezer, which was designated as a city of refuge in the desert plateau. The inclusion of these towns shows that God's covenant care covered the eastern tribes just as fully as the western ones.

The tribe of Gad gave four towns east of the Jordan to the Merarite Levites. These included Ramoth in Gilead, which served as a city of refuge, and historic towns like Mahanaim and Heshbon. Spreading the Levites across the eastern frontier provided steady spiritual leadership for those border regions.

The Merarite families received twelve towns in all, drawn from Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad. With this allotment, every clan within the tribe of Levi had received its assigned dwelling places. God's distribution plan was carried out fully and fairly for every family line.

Altogether, the Levites received forty-eight towns throughout the entire land of Israel. Years earlier, God had commanded Moses to give them exactly this number. Scattering the Levites among all twelve tribes ensured that every community had teachers of God's law living right beside them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The list of forty-eight Levitical cities is viewed as an idealized account written in later centuries when the priesthood was fully established, rather than an exact record of the conquest era.

notes.meaning: Every single town given to the Levites included surrounding pasturelands for their herds. The Levites did not farm large tracts of land like the other tribes, so these grazing fields were essential for their daily needs. God generously supplied food and space for those devoted to His service.

other.view: The list of forty-eight Levitical cities is viewed as an idealized account written in later centuries when the priesthood was fully established, rather than an exact record of the conquest era.

notes.meaning: The Lord gave Israel all the land He had sworn to their ancestors, and the people took possession and settled down. God gave them full ownership of the entire territory and destroyed any organized resistance that stood against them. The land was God's free gift, given in perfect loyalty to His covenant promises.

differ.view: God gave the whole land in principle and full right, and Israel's failure to drive out every remaining pocket of Canaanites was due entirely to their own lack of faith and obedience.
God gave Israel the title and immediate control over what they needed, but the complete possession of the rest was conditional on their continued obedience and active cooperation with Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: This statement is seen as a theological summary by later biblical editors that idealizes the conquest, since other passages show that many Canaanites remained in the land.

notes.meaning: The Lord gave the people rest from war on every border, just as He had promised to their fathers. Whenever enemies tried to fight them, the Lord gave Israel victory, so no hostile army could stand in their way. This peaceful rest allowed the tribes to settle their families and build their homes without fear.

Not a single good word that the Lord had spoken to Israel failed; every promise came true. This verse stands as the high point of the whole book, celebrating God's total faithfulness to His people. Believers can rest their full trust in God because He always keeps what He promises.

differ.view: God fulfilled His promises completely on His part, and any land left unconquered was caused entirely by Israel's own laziness and lack of courage.
God proved entirely faithful to His word, but the people's ongoing possession of the land remained conditional on their continued obedience.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some use this verse to claim that God guarantees immediate material wealth and physical healing to every believer right now, though older commentaries apply it to God's covenant loyalty and redemptive plan.
